title: Rahul Bhatt Revisits Strained Bond With Father Mahesh Bhatt
excerpt: In a new Indian Express feature, Rahul Bhatt reflects on growing up with an absent father — echoing his father Mahesh Bhatt's own account of a childhood without a father figure.
body:
• The Indian Express has revisited the long-strained relationship between filmmaker Mahesh Bhatt and his son Rahul, framing it as a repeating pattern: Mahesh grew up without a father figure, and Rahul says he experienced the same absence.
  • Rahul Bhatt has said his father "never fulfilled his responsibilities" as a parent — a grievance rooted in Mahesh leaving the family home when Rahul was around three.
  • Mahesh Bhatt has acknowledged the wound in past interviews: "There was a wound there… I left home when he was around three and he felt I had abandoned the family for another woman. And this was a grievance I couldn't deny him because it was true."
  • Rahul has described his father as financially supportive but emotionally absent, telling Hindi Rush in 2025: "I had to be my own doctor, lawyer and therapist. Nobody came to my aid."

The Indian Express this week turned its lens on one of Hindi cinema's most openly fractured father-son relationships: filmmaker Mahesh Bhatt and his son Rahul. The feature, headlined with Rahul's words — "Tried to love him, he could've tried too" — traces a wound that spans two generations. Mahesh grew up feeling the absence of his own father; his son says he grew up feeling the absence of his.

A pattern across generations

Mahesh Bhatt has never hidden the first half of that pattern. Born to pioneering filmmaker Nanabhai Bhatt and Shirin Mohammad Ali, he has described himself as "the bastard child of a single Muslim mother" and spoken of missing a father figure throughout his life. "I started out being a scared father. I didn't have one so I didn't know how to be one!" he once admitted. He has also said he made peace with his father late in life: "I made peace with my father much before the end, because I saw in him my own inadequacies."

That self-awareness did not spare the next generation. Rahul Bhatt — Mahesh's son with former wife Kiran Bhatt, and brother of Pooja Bhatt — has spent much of his adult life describing what it was like to grow up in the shadow of a famous father who was rarely present.

Rahul's account

The rawest version came in 2012, when Rahul spoke to The Times of India around the release of his book Headley & I, co-written with journalist S. Hussain Zaidi. "My father Mahesh Bhatt never treated me like his own child," he said. "It's the raw uncut truth about my relationship with my father. I've put it all in the book. I've exorcized my demons." He described himself as a "super-bastard" child and said the neglect at home had left a vacuum that his unlikely friendship with David Coleman Headley — the Pakistani-American later convicted for scouting targets for the 2008 Mumbai attacks — temporarily filled. "My childhood insecurities, the lack of a father-figure in my growing years were lacunas in my life," he said at the time.

Thirteen years later, the tone had softened but the substance had not changed. In an April 2025 conversation with Hindi Rush, Rahul said his father had been "financially available, but emotionally, we are different people." He recalled being ridiculed by other children over his parents' separation, growing angry and withdrawn, and navigating adulthood without guidance.

"He was financially available, but emotionally, we are different people. I had to be my own doctor, lawyer and therapist. Nobody came to my aid."

— Rahul Bhatt, in conversation with Hindi Rush, April 2025

Mahesh's response

To his credit, Mahesh Bhatt has never denied his son's version. "There was a wound there… I left home when he was around three and he felt I had abandoned the family for another woman," he has said. "And this was a grievance I couldn't deny him because it was true."

He has described the father-son bond as "in tatters" but "never fully broken" — and credits the Headley crisis with forcing a reckoning. When the family came together during that episode, he said, Rahul "realised that the father he thought wasn't there, had never really left. Slowly we began rebuilding our relationship and I urged him to use his anger against me to fuel his goals. And he managed to do that." Rahul went on to build a career as a celebrity fitness trainer — he trained Aamir Khan for Dangal — without, his father says, ever trading on the Bhatt name. "He's an entirely self-made man and I'm very proud of that."

Why the story still resonates

The Indian Express feature lands because it treats the Bhatts' rift not as gossip but as a case study in how family patterns repeat. A man who felt abandoned by his father became, by his own admission, an absent father himself — and both men have now spent decades talking about it in public, an unusual candor in an industry that prefers its family narratives polished.

For readers in the diaspora, the specifics are Bollywood but the themes are universal: migration, divorce and demanding careers separate parents from children in Indian families everywhere, and the question of what a father owes his children — money, presence, or both — is one many households are still working out.
image_caption: Rahul Bhatt in a photograph from around the time of his 2012 interviews. The celebrity fitness trainer has spoken repeatedly about his strained relationship with his father, filmmaker Mahesh Bhatt, a rift revisited this week by The Indian Express.
nri_angle: The Bhatts' story is Bollywood-specific but the themes — absent fathers, divorce, and whether a parent owes money, presence or both — play out in Indian families everywhere, including across the diaspora.
author: Diaspora Desk
